questions.q: Why is the asteroid belt not like a crowded road?
choices: Every asteroid moves in exactly the same direction.
The rocks travel only at night.
There is a great deal of space between most of its rocks.
Cars and buses cannot drive in space.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 1 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: What can scientists learn by observing the same object many times?
choices: They can make it move faster through space.
They can make a better estimate of its future path.
They can change its colour with a telescope.
They can choose a new name for the Sun.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why did the students look at the Moon rather than at an asteroid?
choices: Asteroids cannot be seen with any telescope.
The teacher forgot all the photographs of asteroids.
The club did not have permission to look at planets.
The Moon was easier to see through their telescope.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: What do the old craters on the Moon show?
choices: Space rocks hit it long ago, and the marks stayed.
The Moon has strong winds that make new holes.
Rain often washes the Moon's surface clean.
The craters were built by people who visited it.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why is 'near Earth' not the same as 'about to hit Earth'?
choices: Every object near Earth is already on the ground.
Scientists cannot calculate anything about moving rocks.
An object can pass nearby without travelling into our planet.
A nearby asteroid always becomes a small moon.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: What did the DART experiment demonstrate?
choices: A spacecraft could change a small object's movement.
The spacecraft made the asteroid disappear.
It showed that the Moon has no craters.
A telescope can push a rock away without touching it.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why did Nina feel excited after learning about DART?
choices: It showed that school clubs never need to study the sky.
It showed a possible way people could prepare for a future danger.
It proved that every asteroid will hit Earth.
It let Nina travel to the asteroid herself.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: A newly found asteroid is seen in only one photo. What should a team do next?
choices: Announce that it will certainly hit Earth.
Ignore its movement because it is still far away.
Ask students to choose its orbit by voting.
Take more observations before deciding where it will travel.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: A friend asks why craters are easier to see on the Moon than on Earth. What is the clearest reply?
choices: Earth has never been hit by space rocks.
The Moon has no wind or rain to hide them in the same way.
The Moon has a much faster weather system.
Earth's telescope images are always less clear.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the end of Nina's visit?
choices: Scientists can now stop all possible impacts immediately.
All space rocks can be seen from every school telescope.
Learning about the Moon is unrelated to asteroid research.
Watching and understanding space is the first step towards protecting Earth.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original A2 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.
